issues.description: FAQ example reads req.stream.read(req.content_length or 0) without stating the invariant or termination behavior on short/blocking streams.
issues.detail: The docstring example reads from req.stream (not bounded_stream) using content_length as the byte count. The invariant is unstated: 'we trust the client's Content-Length header to bound the read.' With a misreported larger Content-Length the read could block or hang. Since the surrounding example (things_advanced.py) was specifically changed to bounded_stream, the FAQ should follow the same pattern and state why.

issues.description: Test resp4 asserts a 400 but the underlying mechanism that produces it is not explained in code or comment.
issues.detail: The test sends body='' with Content-Length: 1 and asserts 400. The path to 400 routes through bounded_stream.read() returning b'' and JSONTranslator raising HTTPBadRequest('Empty request body'). A literate test would name this invariant inline so a future reader understands what is being exercised — empty-body-with-nonzero-content-length, not malformed-JSON, not auth failure.

issues.description: FAQ example has dead branch: req.stream.read(req.content_length or 0) inside an else where content_length is already non-None and non-zero.
issues.detail: The outer guard is 'if req.content_length in (None, 0)'. In the else branch content_length is guaranteed truthy, so 'req.content_length or 0' simplifies to 'req.content_length'. The fallback is unreachable. Minor, but Knuth's standard for example code is that every token should mean what the reader thinks it means.

issues.description: Magic literal '1337' in the test path obscures intent; a named constant would make the test read literately.
issues.detail: The user_id '1337' appears in both POST tests with no comment. A reader has to infer that any non-empty path segment satisfies the route. A one-line comment or a USER_ID = '1337' constant near the top of the test would make the test self-explaining, which matters because test_examples.py is documentation-by-example.

issues.description: README diff carries many unrelated cosmetic reformattings that dilute the reviewable change.
issues.detail: The PR's stated purpose is POST tests plus one bounded_stream fix plus an FAQ entry. The README diff additionally reflows string concatenations, swaps %-formatting for .format(), changes resp.status construction, and reorders imports. None are wrong, but they make the diff harder to study as a mathematical object — the load-bearing change is buried under whitespace. Split or note in the PR description.

issues.description: StorageError.handle signature changed from (ex, req, resp, params) to (req, resp, ex, params) in README without explanation.
issues.detail: This is a documented public-facing example and the argument order for falcon error handlers matters to readers copying it. If the framework's add_error_handler signature is (req, resp, ex, params) this is a correctness fix worth calling out; if it accepts both via inspection this is a stylistic choice. Either way, the change deserves a one-line note so a careful reader can verify the invariant 'this signature matches what falcon will call.'

review.summary: The substantive change — switching things_advanced.py to req.bounded_stream.read() and adding two POST tests — is correct and the new test that exercises empty-body-with-nonzero-Content-Length is a genuinely useful regression test. However, the work is UNDER-AUDITED in the literate sense: neither the FAQ example nor the test names the invariant being exercised, the FAQ example uses req.stream (not bounded_stream) inconsistently with the very fix this PR is making elsewhere, and the FAQ snippet contains a small dead expression. The README portion of the diff carries substantial unrelated cosmetic reformatting that dilutes the reviewable surface. Verdict: NEEDS-LITERATE-COMMENT — code path is right, but the explanation a future reader needs is missing in two places.
